blocks.text: First law of thermodynamics is actually a manifestation of law of conservation of energy, which states,

blocks.title: Law of conservation of energy
blocks.text: “Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but can be converted from one form to another.”

Germain Henri Hess applied the law of conservation of energy to enthalpy changes. There are many reactions, for which ΔH cannot be measured directly by calorimetric method. For example, tetrachloromethane CCl₄ cannot be prepared directly by combining carbon and chlorine. Hess’s Law helps us calculating the enthalpy changes for such reactions or processes. It states:

blocks.title: Hess’s Law
blocks.text: “The total enthalpy change in a chemical reaction is independent of the route by which the chemical reaction takes place as long as the initial and final conditions are the same.”

Hess’s law can be illustrated by drawing enthalpy cycles, often called energy cycles or Hess cycles. Let A be converted to ‘B’ directly in a single step, which is the direct route; or in a series of two or three steps designated as indirect route 1 and indirect route 2 respectively as shown in Figure 6.8. The products formed in these routes (M, N and X, Y, Z) are called reaction intermediates.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The cycle described here is Figure 6.4 (Hess’ cycle), printed beside this paragraph; Figure 6.8 is the enthalpy cycle of sodium chloride.

blocks.alt: Hess' cycle. Red box A on the left and red box B on the right are joined by a thick red arrow labelled delta Hr (direct route). Above, green arrows go from A to a green box M + N (delta H1) and on to B (delta H2): indirect route 1. Below, blue arrows go from A to box X (delta H3), from X to box Y + Z (delta H4) and from Y + Z to B (delta H5): indirect route 2. Dashed arrows mark the three routes.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: Hess' cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.4).

blocks.text: Then according to Hess’ law,

blocks.latex: \text{For the indirect route 1: }\ \Delta H_r = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2
blocks.text_alt: For the indirect route 1, we can write: ΔHr = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂

blocks.latex: \text{For the indirect route 2: }\ \Delta H_r = \Delta H_3 + \Delta H_4 + \Delta H_5
blocks.text_alt: For the indirect route 2, we can write: ΔHr = ΔH₃ + ΔH₄ + ΔH₅

blocks.text: Below are few examples of it.
i) Calculating Enthalpy of Formation (ΔH°f) using Enthalpy of Combustion (ΔH°c)

CO(g) + ½ O₂(g) → CO₂(g)    ΔH₂ = –283 kJ mol⁻¹
C(graphite) + ½ O₂(g) → CO(g)    ΔH₁ = ?

blocks.alt: Hess cycle for the formation of CO: C + O2 goes directly to CO2 (delta H); the indirect route goes from C + O2 to CO + 1/2 O2 (delta H1) and then to CO2 (delta H2). Blue curved arrows above and below show the two routes.

ii) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Reaction (ΔH°r) using Enthalpies of formation (ΔH°f)

blocks.title: Sample Problem 6.4
blocks.problem:
Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction of
C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl
Using Hess cycle with the help of following combustion data.
ΔH°f of C₂H₄ = + 52.2 KJ mol⁻¹
ΔH°f of HCl = -92.3 KJ mol⁻¹
ΔH°f of C₂H₅Cl = -109 KJ mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The data given are enthalpies of formation (ΔH°f), not combustion data: ΔH = ΔH°f(C₂H₅Cl) – [ΔH°f(C₂H₄) + ΔH°f(HCl)] = –109 – [+52.2 + (–92.3)] = –68.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.alt: Hess cycle: C2H4(g) + HCl(g) goes to C2H5Cl(g) (delta H). Below, a blue box with the elements 2C(s) + 2 1/2 H2(g) + 1/2 Cl2(g); arrows go up from it to C2H4 (+52.2), to HCl (-92.3) and to C2H5Cl (-109). Dotted blue lines lead from the box to C2H5Cl.
blocks.caption: Hess cycle of Sample Problem 6.4 (original drawing after the figure printed on p127 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed cycle of Sample Problem 6.4 leaves out the ‘+’ between 2C(s) and 2½ H₂(g) and prints Cl as ‘CI’; both are written correctly above.

iv) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Formation of a substance (ΔHf°) using Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpies of Formation of other substances

blocks.title: Sample problem 6.6
blocks.problem:
Propane (C₃H₈(g)) burns in oxygen according to the equation:
C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g)
When 14.64 g of propane is burned in an excess of oxygen in a calorimeter at 25 °C and 1 atm pressure, 678.6 kJ of heat is evolved. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propane. The standard enthalpies of formation of CO₂(g) and H₂O(g) are –393.51 kJ mol⁻¹ and –241.82 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.
steps: Solution: The first step is to find the enthalpy change when one mole of propane is burned.
No. of moles of propane = 14.64/44.096 = 0.3320 mol
So, 0.3320 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6 kJ
1.0 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6/0.3320 kJ mol⁻¹ = –2044 kJ mol⁻¹
According to Hess’ law: ΔHr = [3 × ΔH°f (CO₂) + 4 × ΔH°f (H₂O)] – [1 × ΔH°c (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°c (O₂)]
Taking the heat of combustion of O₂(g) to be zero and solving this equation for ΔH°f (C₃H₈) gives,

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the Hess sum the reactant terms are enthalpies of formation, not of combustion: [1 × ΔH°f (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°f (O₂)], and it is the enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) that is zero, because O₂ is an element in its standard state. Solving gives ΔH°f (C₃H₈) = –104 kJ mol⁻¹, as the book finds.

blocks.text: v) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Reactions (ΔHr) using Bond Energies

A special case of Hess’ law involves the use of bond energies to estimate heats of reaction for gas-phase reactions. In the first step, the bonds in all the reactant molecules are broken to give free atoms in the gas phase. The enthalpy change for this step can be calculated by adding the bond enthalpies from Table 6.1. In the second step, the product molecules are formed. The enthalpy change for this step can again be estimated from the bond enthalpies of Table 6.1, which must now be taken with minus sign because the bonds are being formed instead of broken. In general, the heat of reaction for any gaseous chemical reaction can be calculated from average B.E.’s by use of the following version of Hess’ law:

blocks.alt: Triangle: 'Reactants' arrow to 'Products' labelled delta H(o)rxn in red; 'Reactants' arrow down to 'Atoms' labelled E(R); 'Atoms' arrow up to 'Products' labelled E(P).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: Hess cycle; showing the relationship between B.E.'s and delta Hr = sum n ER - sum n EP (original drawing after the textbook's second Figure 6.4).

blocks.title: Sample problem 6.7
blocks.problem:
In the case of formation of HCl(g) from H₂(g) and Cl₂(g), use B.E. data from Table 6.1 to estimate ΔH for the reaction:
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g)
And finally calculate the heat of formation of HCl.
steps: We replace this reaction by a hypothetical two-step process. The bonds in all the reactant molecules are first broken, and then the atoms are combined to make the products.
First Step: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 H + 2 Cl(g);  EH–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹ ; ECl–Cl = 242 kJ mol⁻¹
ER = (1 mol × 436 kJ/mol) + (1 mol × 242 kJ/mol) = 436 kJ + 242 kJ = 478 kJ
Second Step: 2 H(g) + 2 Cl(g) → 2 HCl(g);  EH–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹
The standard enthalpy change in the reaction is obtained by the following formula: ΔHr° = ∑ER – ∑EP
blocks.answer: Enthalpy of formation of HCl, = –184/2 kJ = –92 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 436 kJ + 242 kJ = 678 kJ, not 478 kJ; the book’s diagram and the next step (678 – 862 = –184 kJ) use 678 kJ.
The energy cycle is shown below:

blocks.alt: Energy-level diagram. Top level: 2 H & 2 Cl atoms (two blue and two red balls). Middle level on the left: H2 & Cl2 molecules (blue H-H and red Cl-Cl). Lowest level on the right: 2 HCl molecules. A grey arrow up from the middle to the top level: delta HR = +678 kJ. A grey arrow down from the top to the lowest level: delta HP = -862 kJ. A thick black arrow down from the middle to the lowest level: delta Hrxn = -184 kJ.
blocks.caption: Hess' cycle; showing the relationship between B.E.'s and delta H for H2 + Cl2 to 2HCl (original drawing after the figure printed with Sample Problem 6.7, p129 of the textbook).
